questions.question: What is a goroutine, and how is it different from an operating-system thread?
questions.title: Goroutines, threads, and completion
questions.direct_answer: A goroutine is an independently executing function managed by the Go runtime, while an operating-system thread is scheduled by the kernel. The runtime can multiplex many goroutines across OS threads, and goroutine stacks start small and grow. A `go` statement does not wait, so completion still needs an explicit channel receive or `sync.WaitGroup`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that starting concurrent work and waiting for its completion are separate operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Starting work with `go` and assuming the caller or `main` automatically waits for it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the wait operation to both lifecycle control and visibility of completed work.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The Go runtime schedules goroutines over operating-system threads.
The caller continues immediately; it does not receive `f`'s return values.
A goroutine ends when its function returns or the whole process exits.
A channel receive can wait for one result; a `WaitGroup` can wait for a group.
Use cancellation as well as waiting when a goroutine may outlive the work that started it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A goroutine is a function executing independently alongside other work in the same Go process. It is scheduled by the Go runtime, whereas an operating-system thread is scheduled by the kernel. The runtime can map many runnable goroutines onto OS threads, so launching a goroutine does not normally create one dedicated thread.

Goroutines are cheaper units of concurrency because their stacks start small and can grow. They still share the process address space, so ordinary shared-memory races remain possible. Writing `go load()` starts independent execution and lets the current function continue; it gives no guarantee about which goroutine runs next.

For example, two workers can each calculate a subtotal and send it to a buffered result channel. The main goroutine receives exactly two values before printing the total, so completion is deterministic without using `time.Sleep`, even though result order may vary.

A goroutine also has no automatic join operation. I use a result channel when a value matters or a `sync.WaitGroup` when only group completion matters. Every started goroutine needs a finish path and, when work can be abandoned, a cancellation path as well.

sections.title: Runtime scheduling and lifecycle are separate
sections.content:
The operating system schedules threads that can execute on processors. Inside the process, the Go runtime schedules goroutines onto those threads and manages their growing stacks. That extra layer makes it practical to express many independent activities, but scheduling order and exact runtime costs remain implementation details rather than a correctness contract.

A `go` statement then creates a second question: how will the owner observe completion? A successful result receive proves the corresponding send occurred; a `WaitGroup.Wait` proves the registered tasks returned. These explicit events—not thread timing or print order—give the program the ordering it needs. Cancellation separately tells work that its result is no longer wanted.

sections.title: From goroutine to thread and back to completion
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Many runnable goroutines] --> B[Go runtime scheduler]
  B --> C[OS thread 1]
  B --> D[OS thread 2]
  C --> E[Processors]
  D --> E
  A --> F[result send or Done]
  F --> G[Owner receives or waits]
```

sections.title: Wait for results without sleeping
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func square(n int, results chan<- int) {
    results <- n * n
}

func main() {
    results := make(chan int, 2)
    go square(3, results)
    go square(4, results)

    first, second := <-results, <-results
    fmt.Println(first + second)
}
```
The two individual results may arrive in either order, but their sum is always `25`. The receives are the completion points; no timing guess is involved.

questions.question: Why can `main` exit before a goroutine finishes, and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: Preventing unfinished goroutines at program exit
questions.direct_answer: `main` is not a background supervisor: when the `main` function returns, the program terminates and other goroutines do not get an automatic grace period. Prevent early exit by waiting on a meaningful synchronization event, usually a result channel or `sync.WaitGroup`, and propagate cancellation so blocked work can also stop.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to diagnose nondeterministic missing work without relying on delays.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding `time.Sleep` to main and treating a machine-dependent delay as synchronization.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate successful completion, error reporting, and cancellation in the shutdown design.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The process ends when `main` returns, regardless of unfinished goroutines.
Scheduling order is not guaranteed, so a child may not run before exit.
Sleeping only changes probability; it does not prove completion.
Receive a result when data matters, or wait on a `WaitGroup` when only completion matters.
Design error and cancellation paths so waiting cannot last forever.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `main` function runs in the initial goroutine, but it does not own an implicit join operation for every goroutine it starts. Once `main` returns, the Go process terminates. A newly launched goroutine may finish first, run partly, or not visibly run at all, depending on scheduling.

I prevent that by waiting for the event the program actually needs. If a worker produces a value or an error, I receive that result. If several independent tasks only need to finish, I register them with a `sync.WaitGroup`, incrementing before launch and calling `Done` when each task returns.

For example, a program that launches three formatters can collect three results from a channel and print them in input order after all have arrived. That is deterministic even though execution is concurrent. A sleep such as 100 milliseconds can pass locally and fail on a slow CI machine.

Waiting must also have an exit path for failure. In a server or command, I pass a `context.Context` to cancellable work, stop launching new tasks after cancellation, and still wait for the started tasks to return before the owner exits.

sections.title: A sleep is delay, not evidence
sections.content:
The bug often looks random because printing is itself observable work. With no synchronization, there is no requirement that the new goroutine reaches its print before `main` returns. Making the delay longer hides the missing contract and makes tests slower; it cannot cover every scheduler, machine load, or I/O pause.

A correct shutdown has explicit accounting. The owner knows how many tasks it launched, how each task reports success or failure, and how to tell remaining tasks to stop. It waits for the same set it started. This also prevents another failure mode: returning early on the first error while other goroutines remain blocked trying to send results nobody receives.

sections.title: Choose the completion signal
sections.content:
| Need | Appropriate mechanism | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| One computed value | Result channel | A value was produced and transferred |
| Several tasks finished | `sync.WaitGroup` | Every registered task returned |
| Stop work early | `context.Context` | Cancellation was requested, not that work has stopped |
| Wait a fixed delay | `time.Sleep` | Only that time elapsed; no completion guarantee |
